editorial_contributions.text:
The chromatic number of the plane (CNP) is the minimum number of colors required to color the plane in such a way that there exists no monochromatic pair of points with distance \(1\). The problem was posed around 1950 and the early work on CNP showed that the chromatic number is between \(4\) and \(7\). The lower bound is due to the Moser Spindle graph, a \(7\)-vertex unit-distance (UD) graph with \(11\) edges. In a UD graph, the vertices are points in the plane and they are connected by an edge whenever the distance between them is exactly \(1\). The upper bound can be shown by a tessellation of the plane using hexagon tiles for which the maximum distance within a tile is slightly smaller than \(1\). Each tile has a single color and tiles of the same color can be placed more than distance \(1\) from each other.

\textit{A. D. N. J. de Grey} [Geombinatorics 28, No. 1, 18--31 (2018; Zbl 1404.05063)] improved the lower bound of CNP by constructing a 1581-vertex UD graph with chromatic number \(5\). Several interestig results followed but existing techniques appear insufficient to construct unit-distance graphs with chromatic number \(6\), if they exists. Important insights might come from odd-distance (OD) graphs, in which two points are connected by an edge whenever the distance between them is odd. To encourage research in this direction, the authors pose the challenge of constructing an odd-distance graph of chromatic number \(6\) or proving that it doesn't exist. Furthermore, a \(5\)-chromatic unit-distance graph of 1441 vertices without Moser Spindles is presented.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The Hadwiger-Nelson problem asks for the minimum number of colors required to color the plane such that if two points are unit distance apart from each other, then those points have different colors \textit{H. T. Croft} et al. [Unsolved problems in geometry. New York etc.: Springer-Verlag (1991; Zbl 0748.52001)]. It has been shown that the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane is 5, 6, or 7 (see [H. T. Croft, loc. cit.] and [\textit{A. De Grey}, ``The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1804.02385}]). Versions of this problem for the hyperbolic plane are investigated in [\textit{E. De Corte} and \textit{K. Golubev}, ``Lower bounds for the measurable chromatic number of the hyperbolic plane'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1708.01081}] and [\textit{H. Parlier} and \textit{C. Petit}, ``Chromatic numbers for the hyperbolic plane and discrete analogs'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1701.08648}]. In this paper, we answer this question for the Taxicab plane. In particular, we show that the minimum number of colors necessary to color the Taxicab plane such that no two points unit distance apart have the same color is four. We do this by tiling the plane using taxicab circles, all of which have radius \(r=1/2\). All the points in the interior of a given circle are colored using the same color. However, the interiors of adjacent circles are colored using different colors, and the boundary of each circle is colored using all four of the colors. This is done in such a way that points on opposite sides of a circle are colored using different colors.

editorial_contributions.text:
This is a presentation of geometry for a reader willing to follow a text with formulas, new concepts, diagrams, and computations, but who does not need to follow any specifically analytical computations (so, no derivatives and no integrals).

Various geometries are presented, each with particularly engaging examples of problems that are formulated in that particular geometry.

After a short chapter that addresses the question ``What is geometry?'' by presenting a survey of the chapters to follow, the reader is introduced to what might be the most familiar territory: Euclidean geometry. There one finds a standard presentation of the origin of geometry, one that ignores Abraham Seidenberg's hypothesis of a ritual origin of geometry, espoused in [\textit{A. Seidenberg}, Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 1, 488--527 (1962; Zbl 0109.00201); Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 18, 301--342 (1978; Zbl 0392.01002)]: ``The cultures that grew up in the arid region of Mesopotamia within the Tigris-Euphrates river system from the 4th millennium BC needed to tackle problems which we would now call geometrical.'' (p.\ 7)

It is followed by Euclid's postulates, ruler and compass constructions of angle bisection and line trisection, mention of the impossibility of angle trisection, the definition of a metric and of an isometry, proof of the irrationality of \(\sqrt{2}\), mention of the fact that \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is not constructible with ruler and compass, that \(\pi\) is transcendental, constructibility of regular polygons and Fermat primes, periodic and aperiodic (Penrose) tilings of the plane, Platonic solids are described -- with the mention on p.~31 that ``The Platonic solids occur in nature: the tetrahedron, cube, and octahedron appear in crystal structures, and all five appear as shapes of some micro-organisms and viruses.'' which was an accurate statement with the state of chemical knowledge in 1948, when \textit{H. S. M. Coxeter} wrote in [Regular polytopes. London: Methuen \& Co. (1948; Zbl 0031.06502)]: ``The tetrahedron, cube and octahedron occur in nature as crystals (of various substances, such as sodium sulphantimoniate, common salt, and chrome alum, respectively). The two more complicated regular solids cannot form crystals, but need the spark of life for their natural occurrence. Haeckel observed them as skeletons of microscopic sea animals called radiolaria, the most perfect examples being \textit{Circogonia icosahedra} and \textit{Circorrhegma dodecahedra}.'' (p.~13), but not in 2021, for it has long been known that icosahedra appear as structures composed completely of boron atoms (icosahedral B\(_{12}\)) and dodecahedra as the boron carbide crystal (linear rods consisting of three carbon atoms and twelve boron atoms arranged in a dodecahedral pattern). The notion of area, analytic geometry, vectors, L. M. Kelly's proof of the Sylvester-Gallai theorem, the question regarding the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane (where the result in \textit{A. D. N. J. de Grey} [Geombinatorics 28, No. 1, 18--31 (2018; Zbl 1404.05063) is mentioned for the proof that the chromatic number of the plane is at least \(5\); \textit{G. Exoo} and \textit{D. Ismailescu} [Discrete Comput. Geom. 64, No. 1, 216--226 (2020; Zbl 1445.05040)] have lowered the number of points required to show that four colors do not suffice, from de Grey's 1581 to 627).

Chapter 3 presents non-Euclidean geometry. First spherical geometry, with an emphasis to mapmaking, Mercator's projection, and a derivation of the area formula for spherical triangles. Then hyperbolic geometry, Poincaré model and Beltrami-Cayley-Klein model, the pseudosphere, deriving the formula for the area of a triangle. Chapter 4 is on differential geometry, all the way to Riemannian geometry (on page 80, there is a typo, Nash's embedding theorem was proved in 1956, not 1966).

Chapter 5 is on projective geometry, its connection with art, conics, the Desargues, Pascal, Brianchon theorems, duality. At the end of this chapter, on page 101, one finds the only misleading statement in the whole book:

``Research in projective geometry declined in the second half of the 20th century, and the subject has all but disappeared from schools.

However, the last three decades have seen a renaissance of projective geometry in both applied and pure forms. An example of the former is the problem of reconstructing a three-dimensional scene from a sequence of two-dimensional images in computer graphics.

[\(\ldots\)]

In pure mathematics, research has focused on projective differential geometry, where properties of curves and surfaces (generalizing projective lines and planes) are studied on general manifolds [\(\ldots\)]''

There is no doubt that the statement that ``research in projective geometry declined in the second half of the 20th century'' is inaccurate, for it ignores the fact that the second half of the 20th century has been the \textit{Golden Age of projective geometry}. The author appears to confuse the question whether a field is fashionable or ``mainstream'' with the question regarding progress in understanding more deeply a certain field. While projective geometry has not been fashionable, nor mainstream during the second half of the 20th century, research in projective geometry during that period has dwarfed the previously achieved knowledge. The whole subject of topological projective planes owes its very existence to the second half of the 20th century, with \textit{H. Salzmann} et al. [Compact projective planes. With an introduction to octonion geometry. Berlin: de Gruyter (1996; Zbl 0851.51003)] collecting many of its spectacular achievements. Projective Klingenberg planes, projective Hjelmslev spaces, the axiomatization of projective Barbilian spaces, projective remoteness planes owe their existence to and were studied intensely in the second half of the 20th century. Lineations between projective planes, such as those studied in \textit{D. S. Carter} and \textit{A. Vogt} Collinearity-preserving functions between Desarguesian planes. Mem. Am. Math. Soc. 235, (1980; Zbl 0444.51004)] showed up during that period. Foundational matters regarding projective planes were sorted out to a great extent during that same second half of the 20th century, as one can read from \textit{G. Pickert} [Projektive Ebenen. 2. Aufl. Berlin-Heidelberg-New York: Springer-Verlag (1975; Zbl 0307.50001)] and in the survey by the reviewer and \textit{C. Schacht} [Dani, S. G. (ed.) et al., Geometry in history. Cham: Springer. 355--399 (2019; Zbl 1454.01016)]. Finite projective geometry is another area that owes its very existence as a research topic to the second half of the 20th century. \textit{J. W. P. Hirschfeld}'s books [Projective geometries over finite fields. Oxford Mathematical Monographs. Oxford: Clarendon Press, Oxford University Press (1979; Zbl 0418.51002); Finite projective spaces of three dimensions. Oxford: Clarendon Press (1985; Zbl 0574.51001)], and (with \textit{J. A. Thas} [General Galois geometries. 2nd edition. London: Springer (2016; Zbl 1358.51002)], together with their bibliographies witness the wealth of results obtained in this area.

The ``focus'' on ``projective differential geometry'' that the author finds to have emerged during ``the last three decades'' is likely to be connected with his own research, such as (with \textit{R. Bryant} and \textit{M. Eastwood}) [J. Differ. Geom. 83, No. 3, 465--500 (2009; Zbl 1196.53014)].

Chapter 6 is on the Erlangen Programme, where affine geometry is introduced, Wiles' proof of Fermat's Last Theorem is mentioned, and the following problem of Steinhaus. ``Does there exist a square with integer sides and a point \(P\) in the plane of this square such that the four distances from \(P\) to the vertices of the square are integers?'' is mentioned as an easy to state, yet unsolved problem.

Chapter 7 is on the author's specialty, the geometry of the physical world, special and general relativity, Aristotelian, Galilean, and Minkowski space-time, pseudo-Riemannian metrics, the Schwarzschild metric, black holes, event horizons, the discovery, on 10 April 2019, of a black hole of mass exceeding six billion solar masses in the centre of the M87 galaxy, whose event horizon is about 18 billion kilometres from its centre. the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems, and twistor theory.
